cheatsheet:
## Words this track uses

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| replica | one copy of the data, on its own machine |
| leader (primary) | the copy that accepts writes and puts them in order |
| follower (standby, secondary) | a copy that applies the leader's changes in the same order |
| log position | how far into the leader's list of changes a copy has got (PostgreSQL calls it an LSN) |
| lag | how far a follower is behind the leader, in changes or in time |
| failover | making a follower the new leader when the old one dies |
| acknowledged write | a write the client was told succeeded |
| concurrent writes | two writes where neither writer knew about the other |
| quorum | a group of replicas big enough to share a member with every other such group |

## Three ways to keep copies

| | Single leader | Many leaders | Leaderless |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who accepts a write | one leader (per shard, a slice of the data) | a leader per region or device | any node, the coordinator, which sends it to all N copies |
| Order of writes | the leader's log | each leader's own log; the leaders copy each other's | none; timestamps or version vectors decide |
| Main risk | a failover loses writes that weren't copied yet; two leaders at once (split brain) | write conflicts; rules can only be checked against a local copy | stale reads; concurrent writes merged or lost |
| Examples | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Kafka, DynamoDB per partition | DynamoDB global tables (MREC), pgactive, sync engines | Dynamo, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak |

## When is a write done?

| Mode | The client hears OK when | A failover can lose | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Asynchronous | the leader has it | every write the new leader hadn't received | the default in PostgreSQL and MySQL |
| Semi-synchronous | one follower has it | nothing, until the follower is slow | MySQL quietly stops waiting after a timeout (10 s by default) |
| Fully synchronous | every follower has it | nothing | one dead follower stops all writes |
| Quorum (W of N) | W replicas have it | nothing acknowledged, if reads use R with R + W > N | a write that timed out isn't undone |

PostgreSQL's `synchronous_commit`, with a synchronous standby: `off` (no wait, not even for the leader's own disk), `local` (the leader's disk), `remote_write` (the standby's operating system has it), `on` (the standby has it on disk), `remote_apply` (the standby has replayed it, so queries there see it).

## Replication logs

| Log | Carries | Breaks on | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Statements | the SQL text | `NOW()`, `RAND()`, auto-increment, triggers | old MySQL, VoltDB (which only runs statements that give the same result everywhere) |
| Physical WAL | the changed bytes of each page on disk | different major versions | PostgreSQL streaming, Oracle |
| Logical rows | each row inserted, updated or deleted, with its key | heavier than the WAL | MySQL row binlog, PostgreSQL logical replication, change data capture |

## Reading from followers that lag

| Anomaly | What the user sees | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Read-your-writes | pays, reloads, and the payment is missing | remember the log position of my last write; read only from a copy at or past it, otherwise from the leader |
| Monotonic reads | the capture appears, then disappears | remember the highest position I've seen, or stick to one follower |
| Consistent prefix | a capture shows up before its authorization | keep related writes in one log (one shard per payment) |

## Many leaders (lesson 5)

- Topologies: a circle, a star, or all-to-all (every leader sends straight to every other). Origin ids stop a change going round forever (PostgreSQL: `origin = none`). All-to-all lets an UPDATE overtake its INSERT; timestamps can't fix that, but holding a change until what it depends on has arrived can.
- Handling a conflict: avoid it (give each record a home region), last write wins (lesson 5's lab: 1% of writes lost with writes 5 s apart, 38.5% at 50 ms), or keep both versions as siblings and merge them. Rules such as "balance at zero or above" or "each key used once" need agreement before the commit.

| | waits for another region | doesn't wait |
|---|---|---|
| one writer per row | CockroachDB (Raft per range, `REGIONAL BY ROW`) | Aurora Global Database (a failover can lose a few seconds of writes) |
| several writers per row | DynamoDB MRSC (multi-Region strong consistency: 3 Regions, `ReplicatedWriteConflictException`), MySQL Group Replication (first commit wins, up to 9 members) | DynamoDB MREC (multi-Region eventual consistency: last writer wins per item, conditions checked locally), pgactive |

## Sync engines and shared text (lesson 6)

| Design | Who orders writes | Products | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Server reconciliation | the server, one at a time; clients replay their pending changes on top | Linear, Replicache and Zero, PowerSync | changes are guesses until the server answers |
| Read-path sync | nobody: writes go through your own API | ElectricSQL shapes | no writes while offline |
| Operational transformation | usually a central server | Google Docs | slow to merge branches that drifted far apart (one trace: an hour) |
| Text CRDT | nobody | Automerge, Yjs | an id for every character, and deleted marks kept forever (Automerge 2: 700 MB for Moby Dick; Automerge 3: 1.3 MB) |

## Leaderless (lesson 7)

| N | W | R | Read sees the last acknowledged write? | Writes survive | Reads survive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 1 | no | 2 down | 2 down |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | yes (Dynamo's common choice) | 1 down | 1 down |
| 3 | 3 | 1 | yes | 0 down | 2 down |

Catching up: hinted handoff (Cassandra `max_hint_window`, 3 h), read repair (only keys that get read), anti-entropy with Merkle trees (`nodetool repair`, before `gc_grace_seconds`, 10 days, runs out). Quorums still miss with sloppy quorums, timed-out writes that landed, concurrent writes, reads during a write, and replicas restored from old data. `Unavailable` means not attempted; `WriteTimeout` means unknown.

## Concurrent writes (lesson 8)

- A happens before B if B's writer knew about A. Concurrent: neither did. It's about knowledge, not time.
- Last write wins drops one of two concurrent writes. Jepsen, on Riak: 71.7% of acknowledged writes lost with no fault, 91.4% with a network partition, none with siblings merged as a set. It's safe only for keys written once.
- Version vectors keep one counter per replica. All entries at most the other's: an ancestor. Each bigger somewhere: concurrent, so keep both as siblings.
- CRDTs: G-Counter (the bigger number per slot), PN-Counter (two G-Counters), OR-Set (unique tags; a remove deletes the tags it saw). No CRDT keeps a rule like "balance at zero or above".

## Numbers worth remembering

| | |
|---|---|
| Round trip across the Atlantic | about 70 ms |
| Dynamo's speed target | 300 ms for 999 of every 1,000 requests |
| Dynamo carts seeing a single version | 99.94% of requests |
| Cassandra hint window | 3 hours |
| How long Cassandra keeps a delete marker (tombstone) | 10 days |
| DynamoDB MREC copies a write to other Regions | typically within a second |
| One frame of a screen at 60 Hz | 16 ms |
recap: Copies on other machines survive a dead computer, answer questions near the people asking, and share the reads. All the difficulty is in the changes, not the data.

Single leader: one leader puts every change in a numbered log, and followers apply it in order. Asynchronous copying says OK first and can lose acknowledged writes on failover; waiting for every follower lets one slow follower stop all writes; semi-synchronous sits in between, and may quietly stop waiting.

A replication log carries statements (which come out differently on a follower for anything like `NOW()`), physical page changes (which tie every copy to one version) or logical row changes (which any version can apply, and which change data capture reads).

A follower that runs behind breaks read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix. The fix is the same idea each time: carry a log position and never read below it, or keep related writes in one log.

Many leaders put a leader in each region or on each device: writes stay local, and a region can fail without stopping them, but two leaders can change one row. Conflicts are avoided with a home region, settled by last write wins (which loses writes), or kept as siblings and merged.

A sync engine keeps a copy on the device. With server reconciliation, the server orders and checks every change while clients replay theirs on top; shared text needs operational transformation (through a server) or a text CRDT (an id per character, no server).

Leaderless stores send every write to N replicas and wait for W; a read asks R. R + W > N makes reads meet acknowledged writes, but it doesn't make the copies act as one. Hints, read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy bring stale copies back.

Concurrency is about what each writer knew, not the clock. Last write wins drops one of two concurrent writes (71.7% in Jepsen's Riak test); version vectors spot them, and CRDTs merge counters and sets without loss, but no merge keeps a rule like a balance at zero or above.

quiz.q: A PostgreSQL primary, the leader, copies its changes asynchronously to one standby. It tells the client a refund succeeded at 10:00:00.000 and crashes 50 ms later. The standby is promoted, made the new primary. What can happen to the refund?
options: It's safe: a confirmed commit is always on the standby
It may be lost: asynchronous copying confirmed it before the standby had it, so the new primary may never have received it
It's applied twice, once by each server
The promotion waits until the old primary comes back and hands it over
quiz.why: Asynchronous means the client hears OK once the primary's own log, the WAL, is safely on its disk; sending the change to the standby happens after that. A crash inside that gap loses confirmed writes on failover. Synchronous commit to the standby (`on` or `remote_apply`) closes the gap, at the price of one round trip per commit.

quiz.q: A leader copies the statement `UPDATE holds SET expires_at = NOW() + interval '7 days' WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042'` to its followers as SQL text, for each follower to run again. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: every follower runs the same statement and gets the same rows
The followers reject it, because statements can't be copied
Each follower works out `NOW()` when it runs the statement, so the expiry times differ from the leader's; sending the changed rows with their values fixes it
The statement runs twice on the leader
quiz.why: Copying statements breaks on anything that can give a different answer each time it runs: `NOW()`, `RAND()`, auto-increment numbers in inserts that run at the same time, triggers. A logical (row-based) log sends the resulting rows, with the values the leader worked out, so every follower ends up exactly the same, whatever its storage format.

quiz.q: A customer pays, and the app reloads the list of payments at once, from a follower that is 300 ms behind. The payment is missing. Which fix lets customers read their own writes without sending every read to the leader?
options: Remember the log position of the customer's last write in the session, and read only from a copy that has got past it, falling back to the leader
Send every read to a random follower, so the lag averages out
Make the follower's cache bigger
Retry the read until the payment appears
quiz.why: The session knows exactly what it needs: everything up to its own write's position. Any follower at or past that position is good enough, and the leader serves only while every follower is behind. Random followers make it worse, and can make data seem to go back in time. Blind retries never end when a follower is stuck.

quiz.q: Authorizations and captures are written to two different shards, two slices of the data, each with its own followers that run behind. A report sees captures whose authorizations don't exist yet. What fixes this?
options: Reading at a stricter isolation level on each shard
Adding more followers to the authorization shard
Setting the clocks of the two shards to agree
Putting all of a payment's events on one shard, so they sit in one log and are applied in order
quiz.why: This breaks consistent prefix: two logs with no common order, read at different lags. Inside one log, the order a follower applies changes in is the order they were committed in, so sending every event of a payment to the same shard makes the problem impossible. Clocks and isolation levels don't create an order between two separate logs.

quiz.q: Which PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit` level makes a COMMIT wait until queries on the synchronous standby can see the change?
options: `on`
`remote_write`
`remote_apply`
`local`
quiz.why: `remote_apply` waits for the standby to replay the commit, so a read there sees it, at the biggest cost in waiting. `on` waits for the standby to write the change to its disk (safe, but not yet visible), `remote_write` only for the standby's operating system to have it, and `local` for nothing beyond the primary's own disk.

quiz.q: A checkout program stores idempotency keys, which mark a request as already done, in a DynamoDB global table in MREC mode, with copies in two Regions. Each request writes its key only if it isn't there yet. A retry with the same key lands in the second Region 200 ms after the first attempt. What can happen?
options: The second write fails with ReplicatedWriteConflictException
Both writes succeed, because each Region checks `attribute_not_exists` against its own copy, and the card is charged twice
The second write waits until the first one has been copied
Nothing: global tables check conditions in every Region
quiz.why: MREC copies writes to the other Regions afterwards, typically within a second, and checks each condition against the local Region's copy. Inside that gap, both Regions pass the check. MRSC would have caught the race and failed one write with ReplicatedWriteConflictException; a home Region per shop would have avoided it.

quiz.q: Three regions copy changes all-to-all, each straight to every other. A capture, an UPDATE, reaches region ap before the INSERT of the payment it captures. Which approach leaves ap right whatever the clocks say?
options: Throw the UPDATE away, because the row doesn't exist
Keep the version with the later timestamp
Switch to a circle, where each region passes changes to the next
Hold the UPDATE until ap has applied everything the capturing region had applied when it made it
quiz.why: The capture depends on the insert, and carrying that dependency (a version vector) lets ap wait and apply both in order. Throwing it away leaves ap disagreeing forever; timestamps get it right only when the clocks happen to agree with the order of events. A circle stops changes overtaking, but then any one region that fails breaks the chain.

quiz.q: A console for disputes, customers' complaints about a payment, works offline. Agent A approves a refund while agent B, also offline, closes the dispute. Which sync design makes sure a closed dispute can't be refunded?
options: Store the dispute in a CRDT, so both edits survive the merge
Last write wins on the dispute row
Server reconciliation: the server runs both changes in one order, with the business rule, and the loser is rejected and undone on its agent's screen
Operational transformation of the two edits
quiz.why: A CRDT promises that the copies end up equal, not that business rules hold: both the refund and the close would survive. Last write wins would silently drop one decision. Operational transformation is for positions in text. Server reconciliation runs the rule once, at a definite point in the order, and tells the agent whose change lost.

quiz.q: A leaderless store keeps N = 3 copies. Writes wait for W = 1 confirmation, and reads ask R = 2 copies. Can a read miss a write that was acknowledged?
options: Yes: 1 + 2 = 3 is not more than 3, so the two copies a read asks may both lack the write
No: R = 2 is a majority
No, as long as hinted handoff is on
Only if two replicas are down
quiz.why: Overlap needs R + W > N. With W = 1, the write may sit on one copy, and the other two make a valid read group that misses it, with every node up. Hints help a down replica catch up later; they don't change the arithmetic.

quiz.q: Two replicas hold versions with version vectors `[(eu, 3), (us, 1)]` and `[(eu, 2), (us, 2)]`. What should a store that uses last write wins do, and what should one that uses version vectors do?
options: Both keep `[(eu, 3), (us, 1)]`, because 3 is the biggest counter
Last write wins keeps whichever has the later timestamp and drops the other; the version vector store sees each is bigger in one entry, calls them concurrent and keeps both as siblings
Both keep `[(eu, 2), (us, 2)]`, because its total is bigger
Both reject the second write
quiz.why: Neither vector is at most the other in every entry (eu: 3 > 2, us: 1 < 2), so neither writer saw the other's write: they're concurrent. Last write wins can't know that, keeps one by clock and silently loses the other. Version vectors spot the conflict and hand both versions to the program, or to a CRDT merge.
